image.alt: A variegated Philodendron Burle Marx in a white pot, its long green leaves splashed and sectored in cream and yellow

light.label: Bright indirect light
light.note: Tolerates medium light, but new leaves come back plainer green

landscape_use.note: Frost-free zones, never in direct sun

snap: The variegated form of the Burle Marx, its long green leaves splashed and sectored in cream and yellow, no two the same. It clumps and spreads instead of climbing, needs brighter light than the plain form to hold its markings, and is toxic to cats and dogs if chewed.

deep_dive.title: Origin & Habit
deep_dive.body: A variegated sport of Philodendron burle-marxii, a Brazilian species named for Roberto Burle Marx, the landscape architect who brought the country's natives into its gardens. It keeps the parent's habit: stems creep and throw offsets at the base, so the plant widens into a clump rather than climbing.

deep_dive.title: Key Care Rule
deep_dive.body: Water when the top inch of the mix has dried, in a loose aroid mix — the thick stems forgive a missed week far better than soggy soil. But light is the rule that decides how it looks: bright indirect holds the markings, too little and new leaves come back plain, too much direct sun and the cream scorches brown.

deep_dive.title: Special Feature
deep_dive.body: The variegation is unstable in both directions, which is the whole appeal and the whole risk. Leaves arrive flecked, half-and-half, or almost entirely cream. A stem that turns fully green will stay green unless you cut it back to a marked node, and an all-cream stem has no chlorophyll to feed itself and will eventually fail.
